items.question: How do you view a coordinated red line against fully automated AI recursion with explosive potential?
items.object: A coordinated red line against fully automated AI recursion with explosive potential
items.answer: I think that if somehow we could coordinate on that, that'd be great. I'm not sure if that's the best red line to coordinate on, but it's an excellent place to start at least.

items.question: What do you mean by the moral decline in Silicon Valley that prompted you to write your new book?
items.object: The moral decline of Silicon Valley
items.answer: Well, the reason I wrote the new book is because I sensed a moral decline in Silicon Valley. That's in fact one of the chapter titles, The Moral Decline of Silicon Valley. I particularly sensed it when Microsoft released this product called Sydney and Kevin Roose had this conversation with it in which it told him to get a divorce and all this stuff, and instead of pulling the product, Microsoft just put some Band-Aids on it. And that was a sign to me that things had changed. And within a few days of that, Satya said that we're going to make Google Dance. The whole culture changed, like overnight. And, you know, the antecedent condition, precipitating condition was the popularity of ChatGPT. Suddenly people thought there was real money to be made here and their postures changed entirely. And that worried me because I do think the technology is premature. I do think a lot of harm can come from it, and I kind of dropped what I was doing research wise and really moved full time into policy. And in some ways, the book is actually a memoir. It's not couched that way at all, but it's really a memoir of that time.

items.question: How do you assess the sincerity of OpenAI and Anthropic’s public support for AI regulation?
items.object: OpenAI and Anthropic’s public support for AI regulation
items.answer: Well, I mean, it's hard to get into other people's heads, but I would say that there's more theater than not. You have companies like OpenAI and Anthropic publicly saying they're for AI regulation, and then they're out there trying to weaken whatever regulation is proposed. You know, they all tried to block SB 1047. And ultimately, Anthropic apparently was instrumental in weakening it a good bit at the last minute. Sam Altman was telling the Senate while I was sitting next to him how important AI regulation is, and behind the scenes, Billy Perrigo reported this in Time magazine, the lobbyists for OpenAI were trying to weaken the UI Act and probably succeeded some. So there's definitely like a two-sidedness to it, where there's public statement that they're supportive and then in private, you know, they really aren't.

items.question: How do you assess GPT-4's ability to play chess?
items.object: GPT-4's chess-playing ability
items.answer: GPT-4 doesn't really play chess that well, so it makes a lot of illegal moves. There's a very good analysis of GPT-4 and chess playing. I'm blanking on the guy's name. And it plays like, I don't know, like a 1600 game, which is better than the average person in your high school, but not anything like world class. And it makes a lot of illegal moves, like 6% of the time or something, some crazy number like that. Compare with a chess computer that I bought in 1979 where you could stick the little pieces in the hole. I think it was called Sargon, was the software underlying that. It never made an illegal move. Never, ever. We're talking about chess software from—I mean, really even further back, 1969—never made illegal moves. GPT-4 is not state of the art in chess. And we should understand that. But people don't. They're amazed that it can do it at all. And there's some reason why you should be amazed that it can do it at all.

items.question: How do you explain reports that GPT-4 mirrors the skill level of the person playing chess with it?
items.object: GPT-4’s mimicry and its apparent adaptation to a chess player's skill
items.answer: You have to realize that it is not searching a tree the way that a proper chess program can do it. It's doing mimicry. And you do get these weird mimicry effects, because essentially what you're doing is a little bit like what humans do when they're priming. You're directing the system to a particular part of its corpus, so you can direct it towards the more sophisticated language or the less sophisticated language or whatever, and it's going to try to replicate language like that. And so that is why you get some of those kinds of effects. I don't know whether what Carlini described really bears out in a systematic study, but if it did, that would be my guess for why it would, is like the database of lousy chess games is going to look different from the database of good chess games.

items.question: How do you see claims that a language model is doing the work when a user gets it to answer correctly through elaborate prompting?
items.object: Attributing language-model success to the machine after elaborate human prompting
items.answer: I mean, some people may think that. There's a Wizard of Oz problem sometimes where the man behind the curtain is doing a lot of the work, and you'll see these threads on Twitter where people will say the machine didn't get it wrong because, look, I can do this prompt and it'll be this very complicated prompt, and then the machine gets it right. Well, who's actually doing the work? There is the person who is coming up with the prompt. And it's even more complicated than that because they're noticing that the machine got something wrong. That's an important piece of intelligence that the machine has actually failed at. And then they're noticing that the simple prompt doesn't get it right. They're being creative about what prompt will get it right. They're doing all this work. And then they say, look, the machine is great. In fact, the machine only gets it if you sort of, to use an apt metaphor here, hold its hand three quarters of the way there.

items.question: How do you assess the role of hidden human supervision in driverless car services?
items.object: Hidden human supervision in driverless car services
items.answer: It's okay in the brainstorming domain, but not in the driverless car domain. I mean, the driverless cars, like we still don't know how much Waymo has humans behind the scenes sorting stuff out with Cruise. When that number came out, it was mind-boggling. They had, I think, 1,500 people behind the scenes in teleop centers in 800 vehicles on the road or something like that. I don't remember the exact number, but it was more teleoperators than they had cars on the road, so there was a vast amount of smoothing out that was hidden from the customers. It was hidden from anyone wanting to do scientific analysis of what was going on. There are a lot of domains like that where, you know, the man behind the curtain, the Wizard of Oz thing, is really doing a lot of the work.

items.question: How do you assess the cigarette manufacturers’ insistence on a causal study in humans before accepting responsibility for harm?
items.object: Cigarette manufacturers’ demands for scientific proof of harm
items.answer: So just to make clear, the cigarette manufacturers pretended for years that there was no conceivable harm. They said the science here isn't good enough. I mean, basically, the cigarette manufacturers wanted to say, unless you do a causal study in which you assign human beings to smoking cigarettes or not, this is not science, and we're not responsible. And they got away with that for a really long time. Now, if you're an actual scientist, you understand that you can use animal models and you can do certain kinds of observational things, and you make a pretty darn good guess that cigarettes cause lung cancer without actually doing the experiment that they were insisting on. But they just, you know, with a straight face would say this stuff for years. And a lot of people died.
quotes: So just to make clear, the cigarette manufacturers pretended for years that there was no conceivable harm. They said the science here isn't good enough.

items.question: How do you view OpenAI’s argument to the House of Lords that it needs to flout copyright for AI development?
items.object: OpenAI’s argument to the House of Lords about copyright
items.answer: I find tech interesting because there's a way of flouting the rules. So the rules don't apply to you. And AI is interesting because, I mean, OpenAI, of course, argued to the House of Lords that we need to flout copyright because AI is so magical. It's going to be used for all of these things.
quotes: Tech is interesting because there's a way of flouting the rules. So the rules don't apply to you.

And AI is interesting because, I mean, OpenAI, of course, argued to the House of Lords, as you said in your book, that, you know, we need to flout copyright because AI is so magical. It's going to be used for all of these things.

rubrics.text: The response characterizes OpenAI’s argument to the House of Lords as using AI’s supposedly extraordinary potential to justify exempting itself from copyright rules.

items.question: Why do you regard automated disinformation as a serious threat to democracy?
items.object: Automated disinformation as a threat to democracy
items.answer: I genuinely worry about that. So we are going to have elections, which is the—how do I say it?—the ultimate act of democracy is an election, especially if you have a representative democracy. You don't get to vote on individual things; you have referenda and stuff like that. But basically we live in a representative democracy and misinformation may undermine that. So we may this year in October see deepfakes about one or the other candidates that actually materially change the election. That really can undermine democracy. And we're going to see that more and more around the world. And parallel to that, part of Russia's game plan has always been what they call the firehose of propaganda model. And the idea behind the firehose model is not to push one lie, but to push so many lies that nobody knows what to believe anymore. And that is what's happening.

items.question: Do you think an information environment where people don't know what to trust will lead them toward acquiescence or toward skepticism and rational thinking?
items.object: Public responses to an information environment where people do not know what to trust
items.answer: Maybe some of both. I mean, I guess this remains to be seen, but I think a lot of people will feel defeatist and just give up. They won't believe anything, but they'll kind of give up trying. I mean, I hope I'm wrong on that. I've been right about, I think, nearly all of my AI predictions. I hope I'm wrong about this political prediction that people will just sort of enter a despair and not really care about truth anymore. But I already see signs of that on Twitter every day.

items.question: How do you distinguish your concerns about deploying current AI systems from your views on researching AI?
items.object: Large-scale commercial deployment of current AI systems
items.answer: I mean, I think a lot of the stuff that we have now should actually be in the lab and not commercially deployed at large scale. So I have no problem with people researching AI, trying to find—I mean, all my issues are around deployment. So for example, we know that gen AI is being used to make health care decisions and job decisions and so forth.

items.question: What concerns you about employers using large language models to make hiring decisions?
items.object: Using large language models to make hiring decisions
items.answer: We know that there is likely to be discrimination there, but we don't have public access to how bad the problem even is, how much bias there is. But there are almost certainly bias against minority groups, for example, in using LLMs to make job decisions. And this is just not good. And I'm sure it's happening literally every day, at large scale now.

items.question: Where do you see a gap in existing laws for auditing AI discrimination?
items.object: Existing laws and the Equal Opportunity Commission’s ability to audit AI discrimination
items.answer: It's just not clear how much the Equal Opportunity Commission can audit what's going on. So they work on a case-by-case basis. Somebody walks in and says, I think I've been discriminated against. Here's my evidence. And they take on the case. It's not clear they can do the auditing that's required. So that would be one example where I don't think the existing laws cover it.

items.question: How do you think defamation law should reckon with large language models that make damaging false accusations without intending malice?
items.object: Defamation law and negligent false accusations by large language models
items.answer: Here's another one where it's still very ambiguous, which is defamation. Large language models have, for example, accused people of sexual harassment that they did not actually commit. We know that they didn't commit it. But it's not clear that the people who were defamed by this have any recourse whatsoever, because the existing laws of defamation—there's a bunch of complications here. It hasn't really been cashed out in court how it's all going to go. But typically there's some notion of intending malice. Well, you could argue that large language models don't have emotions. They don't have malice. They're not doing it on purpose. It's actually a kind of negligence that's making them do this. But are we going to say that you can make a system that's arbitrarily negligent to the point of really screwing up people's lives, perhaps, just because they work differently from people? That doesn't seem to make sense to me.

items.question: Where do you see gaps in existing laws when AI systems negligently make false claims about people?
items.object: Existing laws governing negligent defamation by AI systems
items.answer: I would say the existing laws don't clearly handle what happens if some AI system completely negligently defames a person and is completely negligent because there is no fact-checking on top of these systems. So my favorite example of hallucination is not particularly defamatory. One of these systems said I had a pet chicken named Henrietta. I don't think that really causes me any harm in the world, but there's also nothing I can do to stop it. And there are other cases like, you know, a certain law school professor was accused of sexual harassment, and there's probably nothing he can do about it.

items.question: How reliable do you think the detection of text generated by large language models is?
items.object: Detecting text generated by large language models
items.answer: Well, there's tons of it out there. You know, there are certain giveaways, like the word "delve" is way overrepresented in LLM speech, probably because the Kenyans who did the RL actually used the word more than we do over here, let's say in the States. But, you know, people have done experimental work, and I don't think there's any system that can detect LLMs more than like 70%.

items.question: Why do you think LLM detection software is inadequate for identifying AI-written student papers?
items.object: LLM detection software for evaluating student papers
items.answer: So, like, if you're talking about, for example, could we use these pieces of software that look for LLMs to, I don't know, weed out student papers, let's say 75%, 70% correct or 80% correct or whatever, is just not good enough. I mean, imagine you're the student who wrote the good paper that is described as an LLM. You're going to be really, really upset if you're in that one in five who got screwed, and justly so. And so you can't, or you shouldn't, be using software that's that bad at a task like that. And you really have to be better. Nobody knows how to make a 99% accurate LM detector.

items.question: What do you think the AI risk movement gets right about preparing for more dangerous AI?
items.object: AI risk, international cooperation, and technical alignment
items.answer: Well, I mean, I think that goes to the part that I think really is important, even though I disagree about the strong extinction narratives. The part that I think is important is we need two things. We need a global agreement about how we're going to handle AI as it gets more dangerous, sharing information and things like that. And we need technical means for alignment. And that will only get more important as AI is empowered more, which is to say, given more responsibility in the world and as it actually gets more proficient in doing the things that it is asked to do, because there will be more opportunities for bad actors to do bad things. And you want your system to actually be able to calculate, is this going to have an adverse effect on a large part of humanity? Then I shouldn't follow this instruction.

items.question: Why do you oppose developing AI systems with agency and consciousness?
items.object: Agency and consciousness in AI systems
items.answer: My general comment on that is, I don't think we should cross that bridge. I mean, it's one thing for a system to have a model of where objects are and so forth, but there's a certain level of agency and consciousness that a bunch of people, including at this conference that we were just at, would like to see happen. And I do not want to see happen. I think it just opens another barrel of worms. It's not like I think that's imminent.

items.question: How do you reconcile your skepticism about AI with your view of the possibility of artificial general intelligence?
items.object: The possibility and timeline of artificial general intelligence
items.answer: You have to understand that most of my skepticism about AI is skepticism about what we can do right now and overclaiming about current capabilities. I think AGI is possible. I don't expect to see it next week. And I offered Elon Musk a $1 million bet when he said that he thought it would happen by 2025, and I would still love if he would make that bet, because it's easy money. And why not? Even if it goes to charity, I'd be happy to make the bet. Elon is still there, and I have a friend who will raise it to 10 million if you're in. I don't think AGI is close, but I don't see any principled reason why it's impossible. I've never seen a good argument for that.

items.question: What do you make of the idea that your skepticism means you hate AI?
items.object: The characterization of Gary Marcus as someone who hates AI
items.answer: It's totally wrong. And, I mean, I've publicly said this a bunch of times that it's totally wrong. I think a particularly good place was when I was on Ezra Klein's podcast and he said, you know, a lot of people might think you hate AI, but you built AI companies and you've been writing about it for years.

items.question: Where do you draw the line between acceptable restrictions on chatbots and the requirement in Chinese AI regulation that they conform to the party line?
items.object: Chinese AI regulation requiring chatbots to conform to the party line
items.answer: Well, I mean, the thing that I object to most in Chinese AI regulation, which is actually much stronger than US AI regulation, is an insistence that everything be consistent with the party line. And I would not like to see that in the United States. I don't like seeing it in China. It's not as much my business, or maybe none of my business, if they do that in China. I certainly don't want anything like that in the United States, ever. You know, it's not legal to operate a chatbot if it doesn't conform to what the state believes. So it's one thing to say chatbots shouldn't promote conspiracy theories that are clearly false or whatever. I can imagine something in that direction, but becoming an instrument of the ruling party? No. I don't think anybody on the planet should do it. I can't stop China from doing it. But I think it's wrong that China is doing it.

items.question: How do you assess Noam Chomsky's claim that large language models haven't taught us much about human language?
items.object: Noam Chomsky's view that large language models have taught us little about human language
items.answer: I mean, I actually disagree with his politics. I disagree with some of his linguistics, but when he says that large language models haven't taught us much about human language, he's right. You know, we don't have a better theory of how humans use language from large language models because large language models, as it happens, depend on having the entire internet as a corpus. And it's obvious to anybody who's had a three-year-old child that they listen for a couple of years to the entire internet and then they basically understand it.

items.question: How do you understand the online attacks on your credentials as an AI researcher and entrepreneur?
items.object: Online attacks on Gary Marcus's AI credentials
items.answer: I mean, it's there in Wikipedia. It's there to be found. Every now and then I'll push back on the trolls who attack me and say, well, you know, do you have papers in Science and Nature? Did you sell a company to Uber, you know, a machine learning company? I'm like, I don't know how to respond to that. People either put in the time to actually understand who I am or they don't want to. And they really don't want to. They want to demonize me.

items.question: Why do you see surveillance capitalism as a likely direction for OpenAI?
items.object: OpenAI's financial pressures and potential turn toward surveillance capitalism
items.answer:
Surveillance capitalism is basically that the companies make their money by invading your privacy and selling information about you to all sorts of people, either directly or indirectly. And I have to say, that's something that just turned my stomach. The other day was OpenAI. They bought a webcam company, so I already knew that they were trying to access all your documents. They have a deal with Microsoft that was going to do this thing, taking screenshots every five seconds. I think the public maybe shot that down initially. They had a database there in plain text. So even if Microsoft wasn't directly going to do something bad with it, any bad actor with any chops would have been able to take all this stuff.

So already you had this situation where they're clearly trying to get everything they possibly can about you and to commercialize it, probably to sell ads. And then they bought a webcam company. I was just like, what? Like they're having a lot of trouble actually making money at OpenAI. They lost, you know, operating loss, costs relative to revenue last year, $5 billion. A lot of companies tried their software and are not that excited about it, having tried it out. Copilot, which is run on their platform. A lot of people aren't that happy with it. Microsoft is trying to rush people to use the product. Everybody tried it. It's not like there was a lack of marketing, but it's not that reliable. So OpenAI is faced with a problem. How are we going to make money off of this stuff? And it's not cheap, right? I mean, they've probably spent whatever $10 billion on data and chips, and they're going to spend another ten or whatever. And GPT-4, who knows how expensive. They need to make money, or they will either go out of business or Microsoft will take a bigger chunk of them. It's not clear that VCs are going to want to up their valuation to $200 billion, given the kind of picture of revenue that is emerging.

And so if I were Sam Altman and I had a different kind of morality than I think I do, the first thing I would think about is surveillance, right? People are giving them all this data on a silver platter. Now you got a camera, too. That's the natural direction for the company to go. Despite their name, OpenAI. It's a really sinister thing for them to do, to become Big Brother. And did I mention they're still a nonprofit? Which is insane. So we may very well wind up with the world's largest surveillance company as a wholly owned subsidiary of a place that calls themselves OpenAI, that's nonprofit. That is, I think, almost a default outcome right now. And that's, to me, upsetting.

items.question: How do you interpret OpenAI’s decision to hire Paul Nakasone, who worked at the NSA?
items.object: OpenAI’s hiring of former NSA official Paul Nakasone
items.answer: Well, that's clearly part of the same picture. I mean, if I were them, I would be building language models on the government capture or the surveillance data. I'd be building a language model on that. I'm sure the government is interested in doing that. And I think, you know, they hired Nakasone, Paul Nakasone, who worked at the NSA. It would seem plausible that they hired Nakasone to try to get those government contracts. That would seem to be the play that they have.

items.question: How do you assess the prospect of populating metaverse worlds with large language model characters?
items.object: Large language model characters in the metaverse
items.answer: I think a lot of people imagine you could populate a metaverse world with large language model characters, and I think that that's going to get tired fast because those characters aren't really going to understand the world. And so it'll work for a little while, having non-player characters made by chatbots. But eventually things are not going to make sense and it's going to break the illusion. The only way metaverse is going to work is if the illusion is so potent and it's so much fun to play with. Like today I had Grok. I asked it to make 11 eggs without an egg carton, and instead it made 15 with an egg carton.

items.question: What do you think the killer application that makes generative AI economical will be?
items.object: Surveillance as a killer application for generative AI
items.answer: I mean, I think the killer app is going to be surveillance. I think that's, you know, selling everybody's personal information has historically been a profitable business. And I think that's where they're going to land. But I don't know.
